Su métrica lo admite todo, coplas de soleá, seguidillas o canciones (en Utrera, letras de canciones ajenas): un buen cantaor podría cantar por bulerías la guía telefónica. Cierra cualquier festival en el fin de fiesta, y quien la domina en el cante, el baile o el toque domina todo el flamenco.

scenes.name: Los cantes de ida y vuelta: colombiana, guajira, vidalita, milonga
scenes.book: El flamenco contado con sencillez
scenes.desc: Cantes folclóricos hispanoamericanos (rumba, milonga, colombiana, guajira, vidalita) aflamencados por la manera de cantarlos en Andalucía; fáciles de cantar, no se consideran cante jondo. Llegaron en la última década del XIX y se difundieron desde los años treinta: son la última gran incorporación al flamenco. La idea de que eran cantes andaluces que fueron a América y volvieron es pura mitopoética. Sabicas contaba que él y Vicente Escudero, con muchos contratos en América y el repertorio flamenco agotado, empezaron a tocar esas canciones «con este aire nuestro». La colombiana no viene de América: la creó Pepe Marchena en los treinta, con enorme éxito; Carmen Amaya fue la primera en cantarla y bailarla, Sabicas la tocaba sin nombrarla por vergüenza y Juanito Valderrama popularizó la suya en los cincuenta. La guajira, de Cuba, fue la primera en llegar y la que mejor se adaptó (en Cádiz se cantaban «guajiras festeras» por bulerías); sus coplas son décimas. La vidalita, del norte argentino y triste, la recuperaron en los noventa jóvenes como Mayte Martín; la milonga pampeana la trajo Pepa Oro en compás de tangos, Chacón la remataba por tanguillos y Pepe de la Matrona la grabó. Hay dos discos fundamentales: Cantes de ida y vuelta (Junta de Andalucía, 1985, con Menese, José Mercé y Luis de Córdoba) y Dos mundos cantan (Expo 92, con Valderrama, Rocío Jurado y Chano Lobato).

scenes.name: Las saetas
scenes.book: El flamenco contado con sencillez
scenes.desc: Cante dolido que solo se canta en Semana Santa, al paso de las imágenes, a palo seco o con cornetas y tambores, por martinetes, siguiriyas (las más comunes), soleares, cañas o polos, con coplas de exaltación religiosa que exigen gran potencia de voz. Nace a finales del XIX en Cádiz: Enrique el Mellizo y sus hijos detenían al Nazareno desde los cuatro balcones de su casa con sus saetas. A él se atribuye la saeta por siguiriyas, que desarrolló Manuel Centeno en el siglo XX. Manuel Torre, el Niño Gloria, la Niña de los Peines, Manolo Caracol y Antonio Mairena eran esperados en Semana Santa para cantarlas sin amplificación desde un balcón a la altura de las imágenes; Manuel Mairena grabó un vía crucis entero. Un equipo francés grabó en directo a los saeteros de Jerez, Arcos y Lebrija en la Semana Santa de 1993 para la colección Flamenco vivo.

scenes.name: Demófilo y los Machado
scenes.book: El flamenco contado con sencillez
scenes.desc: Antonio Machado y Álvarez, Demófilo, fue el primer autor español que dedicó un libro entero al flamenco: la Colección de cantes flamencos recogidos y anotados (1881), piedra angular de la flamencología moderna; escribió también sobre las saetas y dirigió la revista El Folclore Andaluz (1882-1883). Sus hijos, los poetas Antonio y Manuel Machado (autor de Cante hondo), heredaron la afición, y sus coplas se cantan a menudo sin que los cantaores sepan que son versos cultos. Calixto Sánchez dedicó a Antonio Machado un disco en 2001, y José Menese hizo suyas las letras de Francisco Moreno Galván.

scenes.name: La farruca y el garrotín
scenes.book: El flamenco contado con sencillez
scenes.desc: Cantes aflamencados de fuera de Andalucía. La farruca, gallega, llegó a Cádiz con los comerciantes gallegos del XIX y es más baile que cante; la popularizó Manuel Torre a principios del XX y hoy casi solo la canta Pepe Menese, con una letra de Moreno Galván que se hizo himno en la Transición. Su baile, viril, lo creó Faíco; Carmen Amaya lo bailó vestida de hombre, Falla lo incluyó en El sombrero de tres picos y la versión de Antonio Gades en la película de Los Tarantos, la última de Carmen Amaya, se enseña hoy en las academias. El garrotín viene del folclore asturiano y lo hicieron suyo los gitanos de Lleida; lo difundieron Carmen Amaya y la Niña de los Peines, que lo cantaba con aire de tangos, Faíco hizo sus coreografías y Blas Vega recogió una copla antigua cantada por el Chaparro en la Magna antología del cante flamenco.

scenes.name: Los fandangos de Huelva
scenes.book: El flamenco contado con sencillez
scenes.desc: Huelva reclama la cuna del fandango andaluz y es la provincia con más estilos: las antologías recogen más de treinta y cinco, locales (Encinasola, el Alosno, Cabezas Rubias, Calañas, el Andévalo, Valverde del Camino) y personales, creados por profesionales como Paco Isidro, Pepe Rebollo, el Comía, Antonio Rengel, Pérez de Guzmán y Paco Toronjo; de fuera dejaron su sello el Gloria, Macandé, el Carbonerillo y Manolo Caracol. Paco Toronjo, fijo en los festivales desde finales de los sesenta y en las bienales de Sevilla, les dio una jondura difícil de imitar. El baile, de pareja y galanteo, se ve ya poco.

scenes.name: Los cantes de Levante o de las minas
scenes.book: El flamenco contado con sencillez
scenes.desc: Nacidos del trabajo en las minas del siglo XIX en las sierras de Cartagena y La Unión y en Linares, La Carolina y Andújar: cantes de dolor profundo sobre la mina, sus accidentes y los compañeros muertos, hechos con fandangos regionales, murcianas, malagueñas y el cante de madrugá de los mineros. La taranta, el más significativo, tiene dos estilos, el de Linares (Gabriel Moreno, Carmen Linares) y el de La Unión (Encarnación Fernández, Pepe Cros), y Camarón le puso dulzura; el taranto, almeriense, tiene compás porque nació para el baile de Carmen Amaya en los cuarenta, con el Ciego de la Playa y Pedro el Morato. La cartagenera, de temas más urbanos, la fijó Antonio Chacón a finales del XIX y la cantaron Cayetano Muriel, Manuel Centeno, Manuel Torre y la Niña de los Peines. La minera se atribuye a Rojo el Alpargatero, Antonio Grau Mora, que hacia 1885 abrió en La Unión una posada que acabó en café cantante y oía cantar a los mineros de madrugada: es el gran creador de los cantes mineros. Las granaínas, de Frasquito Yerbabuena y sobre todo Chacón, son un cante casi barroco hoy cargado de vibratos operísticos. Sin minas, los concursos de Linares y La Unión mantienen vivos estos cantes.

scenes.name: Las cantiñas: alegrías, caracoles, mirabrás y romeras
scenes.book: El flamenco contado con sencillez
scenes.desc: Cantes alegres de la bahía de Cádiz, en compás de soleá y muy ligados al baile, que arranca majestuoso y va ganando fuerza hasta desplantes electrizantes. Nacen probablemente de la jotilla gaditana, hermanada con la jota aragonesa por la resistencia común contra Napoleón, de ahí las letras sobre la guerra y el mar; la leyenda atribuye su creación a Enrique el Mellizo, que oyó a una muchacha cantar jotas con un ciego. Tomaron identidad en la segunda mitad del XIX. Hay cantiñas del Pinini de Utrera y Lebrija y de Córdoba; la rosa ya no se canta. Las alegrías, al principio baile de mujer sola, se hicieron más lentas a comienzos del XX y empiezan con el «tirititrán» que, según Chano Lobato, inventó Pericón de Cádiz al olvidar la letra; las cantaron el Mellizo, Ignacio Ezpeleta, Aurelio Sellés, Manolo Vargas y Pericón. Los caracoles, de Tío José el Granaíno (picador del Chiclanero), los recreó Chacón y triunfaron en Madrid («la gran calle de Alcalá»). El mirabrás son alegrías largas (José Menese, con letras de Moreno Galván), y las romeras se atribuyen al Granaíno o a una cantaora llamada la Romera. Hoy el gran intérprete es Chano Lobato.

scenes.name: Los tangos, tientos y marianas
scenes.book: El flamenco contado con sencillez
scenes.desc: Con bulerías y cantiñas, el gran cante festero: letras de vida, amor y muerte con cierta ligereza, ritmo vivo y pegadizo fácil de seguir con palmas, y un baile sensual. Cádiz y Sevilla se disputan su paternidad, pero los hay en toda Andalucía y en Extremadura; Triana tiene el estilo del Titi y Jerez su propio sello. Su origen musical se discute: Mairena los tenía por cante básico gitano; los estudios recientes los llevan a Cuba y las habaneras llegadas a Sevilla y Cádiz en la segunda mitad del XIX; los granadinos defienden una raíz morisca (el disco Granada canta por tangos recoge trece estilos, entre ellos los de la morería). Manuel Ríos Ruiz concluye que no se sabe con certeza. La Niña de los Peines se hizo inmortal con su copla «Péinate tú con mis peines». Del tango nacen los tientos, más pausados y solemnes, que cantaron primero el Mellizo y el Marrurro y se popularizaron a comienzos del XX, y la mariana, que difundió Bernardo el de los Lobitos y hoy casi solo canta Pepe Menese con letras de Moreno Galván.

scenes.name: Las soleares
scenes.book: El flamenco contado con sencillez
scenes.desc: La madre del cante y uno de sus pilares, independiente de cualquier otro ritmo; los cantaores la consideran «el toro bravo del arte jondo». Coplas solemnes y sentenciosas de tres o cuatro octosílabos, unidas por la guitarra, que suelen rematarse por bulerías; muy apropiadas para el baile de mujer. Se desarrolló al sur del Guadalquivir desde los jaleos festivos: la primera mención es de la Andonda en Triana hacia 1840, una cantaora temible contemporánea del Fillo, y tomó su forma actual entre 1875 y 1915. Las mujeres fueron clave en su creación y transmisión (la Andonda, Mercedes la Serneta, Fernanda de Utrera, Carmen Linares). Hay soleares de Triana (la Andonda, Silverio, Fernando el de Triana, la Niña de los Peines, Tomás Pavón, Mairena), de Alcalá, más solemnes (Joaquín el de la Paula, Juan Talega), de Utrera (la Serneta, el Pinini, María Peña, Fernanda), de Cádiz y el Puerto, más jondas (Enrique Butrón, el Mellizo, Paquirri el Guanté), de Jerez, breves y llenas de melismas (Curro Frijones, José Illanda, Juan Mojama, Tío José de Paula, Manuel Torre) y de Córdoba, más pausadas.

scenes.name: Las siguiriyas, livianas y serranas
scenes.book: El flamenco contado con sencillez
scenes.desc: Una de las expresiones más dramáticas y de los palos más importantes: sin siguiriyas y soleares el flamenco no sería lo que es. Un quejío entero de lamentos que no admite medias tintas («con las siguiriyas no se puede vender la burra»), con coplas trágicas de cuatro versos (6, 6, 10 y 6 sílabas), muchas sobre la muerte de los seres queridos, y falsetas lentas que suenan a campanas a muerto. Lorca la describió como un grito terrible que divide el paisaje en dos; Tía Anica la Piriñaca decía que cuando la cantaba a gusto la boca le sabía a sangre. La cantaban ya el Planeta (la de la Luna, la más antigua conocida) y el Fillo; luego Manuel Torre, Silverio, Paco la Luz, Cagancho, el Nitri, Curro Dulce, el Loco Mateo, el Mellizo, Terremoto de Jerez (que cantó toda la noche por siguiriyas con su madre muerta en brazos) y Juan Talega; hoy el Chocolate y José Menese. Antonio Mairena grabó unas cuarenta y cinco formas: es el siguiriyero más importante. Sus escuelas son Jerez y los Puertos, Cádiz y Triana. En el baile la difundió Vicente Escudero y Pilar López le añadió los palillos. La liviana, cante de campo, caminos y bandoleros, prepara la voz para la serrana, a la que Silverio dio brillo y con la que se remata por siguiriyas.

scenes.name: La caña, el polo y la petenera
scenes.book: El flamenco contado con sencillez
scenes.desc: Tres cantes de la familia de la soleá. La caña, con ayes más arrastrados, se sitúa en la serranía de Ronda (un viajero inglés la oyó allí en 1830) o en la voz árabe gaunia, «canción»; la cantaron el Fillo, Tío José el Granaíno, Antonio Chacón, Pepe de la Matrona y Rafael Romero el Gallina, y hoy se usa más para el baile solemne. El polo se cantaba tras la caña, con la misma métrica; el de Tobalo, su supuesto creador, aparece ya en Estébanez Calderón y hoy se usa en la soleá apolá; Enrique Morente grabó el de Chacón. La petenera, melancólica y de origen incierto, se atribuye a una mujer de Paterna de la Ribera, «la perdición de los hombres», o a los sefardíes de los Balcanes; los gitanos la evitaron porque traía mala suerte. La cantaron la Niña de los Peines, Naranjito de Triana, Rafael Romero, Fosforito y hoy Pepe Menese.

scenes.name: Los cantes de Málaga: malagueñas, rondeñas, jaberas y verdiales
scenes.book: El flamenco contado con sencillez
scenes.desc: Después de Sevilla y Cádiz, Málaga es la provincia con más variedad de cantes. La malagueña, cante libre, sin medida y sin baile, de rico toque, ha influido en las granaínas y en todos los cantes minero-levantinos. Nació en Álora (las malagueñas perotas) a partir de los fandangos abandolaos, acompañados de bandola; tras los anónimos y los de Cipriano Pitana, Francisco Jiménez y Joaquín Tabaco, Juan Breva le dio identidad propia, y Lorca escribió de su trino. Su esplendor es la segunda mitad del XIX, con el Canario, la Trini, Baldomero Pacheco y Fosforito el Viejo; también firmaron malagueñas el Mellizo, único gitano creador de una (inspirada en el prefacio de la misa), y Chacón. Diego Clavel recogió treinta y una en los noventa. La rondeña, de principios del XIX y de la tierra del Tobalo, es la pieza con que muchos guitarristas abren sus conciertos; la jabera, ruda y difícil, debe su nombre a una vendedora de habas y está casi perdida; los verdiales, de probable raíz morisca, apenas han cambiado y conservan la panda con violín, panderos, chinchines y cañas para la fiesta de san Juan.

scenes.name: Los tanguillos de Cádiz
scenes.book: El flamenco contado con sencillez
scenes.desc: Vinculados al carnaval de Cádiz, son el soporte de chirigotas, coros y murgas; cantados en grupo pierden su naturaleza flamenca, que es individual, aunque como baile la conservan. Hay constancia de los «tangos graciosos» del barrio de La Viña en 1779, en la tonadilla La anónima de Tomás Abril, y el tango americano o de negros terminó de formarlos. Letras jocosas y satíricas: «el chiste ingenuo y feliz enfrente de la tragedia jonda del quejío» (Emilio Jiménez Díaz). Aurelio y Pericón de Cádiz, Manuel Vargas y la Perla los grabaron en la primera mitad del siglo XX, y hasta Mairena dejó dos. Chano Lobato, su mayor cultor, los elevó a cante noble y recrea la venta de los cuadros que popularizó Pericón.

scenes.name: Las tonás: martinetes, carceleras y deblas
scenes.book: El flamenco contado con sencillez
scenes.desc: Cantes sin acompañamiento, prueba de su antigüedad, en cuartetas octosílabas de intensa carga dramática y origen gitano indiscutible: son crónicas de la miseria, la cárcel y la persecución. Demófilo ya las daba en 1881 por «cantes viejos casi caídos en desuso»; en el siglo XIX hubo entre veintisiete y treinta y cuatro, cada una con el nombre de su creador. La más antigua es la de Tío Luis el de la Juliana, aguador y primer cantaor del que hay noticia (segunda mitad del siglo XVIII), conservada por Antonio Chacón y recreada por Pepe de la Matrona; se le atribuye también la toná de los pajaritos, que recuerda la tonada sefardí de los bilbilicos. Los martinetes toman el nombre del martillo de la fragua, aunque es difícil cantar mientras se forja: Tío Juane de Jerez montaba una fragua en escena en los setenta y ochenta, y Antonio el Bailarín creó su baile con martillo y yunque; la familia fragüera más antigua es la de los Cantorales de Cádiz, que Silverio visitaba. Las carceleras cantan la prisión y servían para pasar mensajes en romaní desde las rejas. La debla, único palo con nombre romaní («diosa»), es religiosa, casi perdida y muy difícil; llegó a hoy por Tomás Pavón en los cuarenta y la recuperó Antonio Mairena.

scenes.name: Las sevillanas
scenes.book: El flamenco contado con sencillez
scenes.desc: Nacen de las seguidillas castellanas, que en Sevilla se hicieron más vivas y fáciles de repetir: cuatro coplas para bailar en pareja un galanteo, con temas andaluces, amorosos o rocieros (corraleras, rocieras, bíblicas, de feria, marineras, romeras). Lorca recogió una del siglo XVIII. Su gran auge comercial llegó en los setenta, con millones de discos que daban envidia a los flamencos; las han grabado con jondura Manuel Vallejo, la Niña de los Peines, la Paquera de Jerez, el Turronero, Chiquetete y Camarón.

scenes.name: El fandango
scenes.book: El flamenco contado con sencillez
scenes.desc: Muy apreciado por su musicalidad y fácil de interpretar, no es un palo básico pero no es menor: la vieja división entre cantes grandes y chicos está obsoleta, y la jondura la pone el intérprete, no la antigüedad del palo. Canto para bailar de origen muy antiguo e incierto (Corominas lo deriva del portugués fado; hay quien le ve un lejano origen árabe), aparece por escrito en un entremés de 1705 y lo describe el deán Manuel Martí en 1712; en el siglo XIX fue el cante y baile nacional español, y a finales de siglo se aflamencó en Andalucía y dejó de bailarse. De él salen las granaínas, las malagueñas y los cantes de Levante, y hay fandangos propios en Lucena, Cabra, Puente Genil, Jaén, Granada o Almería. Su apogeo en la ópera flamenca lo desprestigió tanto que a cantaores como Pepe Menese les parece un insulto que se lo pidan; desde los años ochenta se revaloriza.

facts.title: 1992 MTV Music Video Awards Altercation
facts.body: The animosity between Nirvana and Guns N' Roses culminated in a backstage altercation at the 1992 MTV Music Video Awards. Axl Rose confronted Kurt Cobain and Courtney Love, reportedly telling Kurt to "keep his woman in line." Simultaneously, Nirvana bassist Chris Novoselic and Guns N' Roses bassist Duff McKagan were also arguing. "This boiled over to an altercation backstage at the 1992 MTV Music Video Awards between Axel, Kurt and Courtney Love."
facts.source: The Ongoing History of New Music
facts.name: Nirvana

facts.title: First Rehab Stint (1992)
facts.body: Kurt Cobain's first trip to rehab was in 1992 after learning he was going to be a father. He stayed for several weeks, but the treatment was ultimately ineffective, as he resumed using drugs upon Nirvana's return from an Australian tour. "His first trip to rehab was in 1992, after he found out that he was going to be a father."
facts.source: The Ongoing History of New Music
facts.name: Nirvana

facts.title: Reading 1992 Performance
facts.body: Nirvana played the Reading festival twice, with their 1992 appearance being recorded and released as a live album. During this performance, Kurt Cobain was rumored to be gravely ill and was wheeled onto the stage in a wheelchair wearing a hospital gown. He then stood up unsteadily, went to the microphone, and the charade ended as Nirvana delivered one of their most memorable performances. "Their 1992 appearance was recorded and released as a live album. This was the gig where Kurt was rumored to be Deathly Ill and he was wheeled on stage in a wheelchair in a hospital gown. He got up, very unsteady, made his way to the microphone. Then the charade was over and Nirvana busted into one of their most memorable performances."
facts.source: The Ongoing History of New Music
facts.name: Nirvana

facts.title: Royalty Dispute Post-Nevermind (1992)
facts.body: In the spring of 1992, after *Nevermind* became a global success, Kurt Cobain decided to unilaterally rewrite the band's royalty arrangements. He demanded 90% of the songwriting royalties, backdated to *Nevermind*'s release in September 1991, and called Dave Grohl and Chris Novoselic "greedy" for wanting a larger cut. After "a bunch of fights," Kurt was eventually "bargained down to 75%" of all material on *Nevermind*. "Things got really heated, especially when Kurt called Dave and Chris Greedy for wanting a bigger cut."
facts.source: The Ongoing History of New Music
facts.episode: Ultra-Deep Background on Dave Grohl: Part 2
facts.name: Nirvana

facts.title: Zoo TV Tour – Pizza Order in Detroit (March 27, 1992)
facts.body: During U2's Zoo TV tour in the early 1990s, a notable incident occurred on March 27, 1992, in Detroit. Amidst the show's characteristic use of TVs with cable/satellite hookups, Bono, using a remote control, chanced upon a commercial for a local pizza place. He then used a cell phone to call Speedy Pizza from the stage, attempting to order "10,000 pizzas" for the 21,064-person audience at The Palace. After the third song, three Speedy Pizza employees delivered 100 pepperoni pizzas, which were subsequently thrown into the chanting crowd. Later, t-shirts featuring the phrase "I'd like to order 10,000 pizzas, please" were sold on the tour's next leg. "That whole exchange happened after the third song in the set."
facts.source: The Ongoing History of New Music
facts.episode: From the Archives: The Top 100 Moments in New Rock - Part 3
facts.name: U2

facts.title: Pixies as Opening Act (1992)
facts.body: The Pixies opened for U2 during their "Achtung Baby" tour in 1992. Although U2 held respect for The Pixies, the audience was not receptive, often leaving arenas and stadiums less than a quarter full during The Pixies' performances. "Everything reached a crescendo during the band's stint warming up for you too during the octangue baby tour in 1992."
facts.source: The Ongoing History of New Music
facts.episode: The Reunions: Some Lasted....and Sadly, Some Didn't ｜ Part 2
facts.name: U2

facts.title: Singles Movie and Soundtrack (1992) Impact
facts.body: The release of the movie *Singles* and its soundtrack in 1992 occurred in a world where alternative and specifically grunge "ruled everywhere." The film, with its music of the moment and cameos from bands like Pearl Jam and Alice in Chains, along with songs played widely on radio and in clubs, played a crucial role in making the "grunge tent even bigger." "And together with the movie, singles made the grunge tent even bigger."
facts.source: The Ongoing History of New Music
facts.name: Grunge

facts.title: Wayne's World Soundtrack Contribution (1992)
facts.body: The Red Hot Chili Peppers were featured on the first *Wayne's World* soundtrack, released in 1992. While the album was primarily composed of classic rock, it notably included tracks from contemporary alternative bands like the Chili Peppers and Soundgarden. "However, it does feature the chili peppers and soundcard."
facts.source: The Ongoing History of New Music
facts.name: The Red Hot Chili Peppers

facts.title: Lollapalooza 1992 Main Stage Act
facts.body: The Red Hot Chili Peppers were among the major bands performing on the main stage of the 1992 Lollapalooza Festival, a lineup described as one of the best in the event's history. "the Red Hot Chili Peppers were there."
facts.source: The Ongoing History of New Music
facts.name: The Red Hot Chili Peppers

facts.title: Frusciante's First Departure and Tour Cancellation (May 1992)
facts.body: The deteriorating internal dynamics within the Red Hot Chili Peppers, exacerbated by John Frusciante's aversion to fame and drug use, culminated in his refusal to perform at Sonic City in Japan on May 7, 1992, declaring he quit. This departure, which the band attributed to Frusciante's mental stress, forced the cancellation of remaining tour dates, including major festival appearances, as an attempt to bring in replacement guitarist Arik Marshall for rehearsals failed due to lack of time. "So the remaining shows in the tour, including a bunch of big festival dates, were canceled."
facts.source: The Ongoing History of New Music
facts.episode: The Long Strange Trip of John Frusciante Part 1
facts.name: The Red Hot Chili Peppers

facts.title: Post-Frusciante Guitarists and Internal Struggles (1992-1997)
facts.body: Following John Frusciante's initial departure, the Red Hot Chili Peppers briefly brought in Arik Marshall, who performed with them at Lollapalooza 1992. After Marshall, Jane's Addiction guitarist Dave Navarro was brought in for one album, but his tenure ended unhappily, and he was fired in April 1997. During this period, Anthony Kiedis continued to struggle with sobriety, and Flea was undergoing a messy divorce, adding to the band's stresses. "Dave Navarro was brought in for one album. That's a whole other story that had an unhappy ending."
facts.source: The Ongoing History of New Music
facts.episode: The Long Strange Trip of John Frusciante Part 1
facts.name: The Red Hot Chili Peppers

facts.title: Eddie Vedder, Chris Cornell, and Al Jourgensen – Bile Beer Drinking Contest at Lollapalooza 1992
facts.body: The 1992 Lollapalooza tour featured the Jim Rose Circus sideshow, including performer Matt "the Tube" Crowley, who would pump beer, ketchup, chocolate, and Pepto-Bismol into his stomach via a seven-foot swallowed tube and then pump it back out as "bile beer" for audience members to drink. Eddie Vedder, Chris Cornell (Soundgarden), and Al Jourgensen (Ministry) entered a competition for who could drink the most bile beer. Cornell tried and retched; Jourgensen managed it two days in a row; Eddie was there every single night and claimed to have drunk two quarts more than anyone. When asked why, Eddie said: "Just looking for attention." "Eddie won this contest. He called it Wayne."
facts.source: The Ongoing History of New Music
facts.name: Pearl Jam

facts.title: Singles Cameo (1992) – Eddie, Stone, and Jeff as Citizen Dick Members
facts.body: In Cameron Crowe's Seattle-set film *Singles* (filmed 1991, released 1992), Eddie Vedder, Stone Gossard, and Jeff Ament appear as the backing band for fictional singer Cliff Poncier (played by Matt Dillon), in a band called Citizen Dick. Their longest appearance is just over a minute, showing them reading a review of their record. By the time the film was released, Pearl Jam was enormous, which worked greatly in the film's favor. Pearl Jam also contributed two songs to the soundtrack: "Breath" and "State of Love and Trust." "By the time the movie was released in 1992, the band was huge."
facts.source: The Ongoing History of New Music
facts.name: Pearl Jam

facts.title: Bile Beer Drinking Contest – 1992 Lollapalooza, Jim Rose Circus, Matt "the Tube" Crowley
facts.body: The 1992 Lollapalooza tour featured the Jim Rose Circus sideshow, including Matt "the Tube" Crowley, who would swallow a seven-foot hose connected to a hand pump, force beer, ketchup, mustard, chocolate, and Pepto-Bismol into his stomach, then pump it all back out into glasses for audience members to drink. At one stop on the tour featuring both Pearl Jam and Soundgarden, Eddie Vedder and Chris Cornell entered a competition to see who could consume the most of this bile cocktail. Eddie won decisively and named his victory "Wayne." "Eddie won this contest. He called it Wayne."
facts.source: The Ongoing History of New Music
facts.name: Pearl Jam

facts.title: Cameo in Singles (1992)
facts.body: Pearl Jam made a cameo appearance in the 1992 Hollywood motion picture *Singles*. The film was significant for not only featuring the music of the moment but also including appearances from prominent bands and figures of the burgeoning alternative and grunge scene, helping to expand grunge's reach. "It was a Hollywood motion picture that not only featured the music of the moment, but also cameos from Pearl Jam and Chris Cornell and Allison Chains."
facts.source: The Ongoing History of New Music
facts.name: Pearl Jam

facts.title: Singles Soundtrack Contribution (1992)
facts.body: Songs from Pearl Jam were heavily played on the radio and in alternative clubs throughout late 1992, following the release of *Singles*. The movie and its soundtrack were instrumental in expanding the reach and popularity of grunge music. "Songs from Allison Chains, Pearl Jam, The Screaming Trees and The Smashing Pumpkins were all played on the radio and in alternative clubs."
facts.source: The Ongoing History of New Music
facts.name: Pearl Jam

facts.title: Lollapalooza 1992 Main Stage Act
facts.body: Pearl Jam was among the major bands performing on the main stage of the 1992 Lollapalooza Festival, a lineup described as one of the best in the event's history. "Sound garden, Pearl Jam, ministry, ice cube. That was just the main stage."
facts.source: The Ongoing History of New Music
facts.name: Pearl Jam

facts.title: Regurgitation Cocktail Drinking Contest (1992)
facts.body: During the 1992 Lollapalooza tour, Eddie Vedder engaged in a drinking contest with Chris Cornell, consuming a cocktail of goo, bile, and Matt "The Tube" Crowley's half-digested last meal, which Crowley had regurgitated on command from a seven-foot hose. Eddie Vedder famously won this contest. "And for the record and for all time, Eddie won this contest."
facts.source: The Ongoing History of New Music
facts.name: Pearl Jam

facts.title: 1992 Seattle Free Show Ticketing Dispute
facts.body: In May 1992, Pearl Jam planned a free show in Seattle for approximately 30,000 people and approached Ticketmaster to handle the ticketing, as city requirements mandated monitoring the crowd size. Ticketmaster quoted costs of $1 to $1.50 per ticket, which would amount to $45,000 for the band to absorb. Pearl Jam ultimately decided not to use Ticketmaster for this event, a decision that marked the beginning of their significant conflict with the ticketing giant. "In the end, for this particular show, Pearl Jam elected not to use ticket master, but the experience somehow left a bad taste in their mouth. And this was the beginning of a fight."
facts.source: The Ongoing History of New Music
facts.episode: The Weird History of Concert Tickets Part 2
facts.name: Pearl Jam

facts.title: Popularity in Late 1992
facts.body: By late summer 1992, Pearl Jam's popularity had surged, contributing to the success of Temple of the Dog, a side project they collaborated on in 1991. The tribute album broke into the top 10 of the album chart and belatedly achieved platinum status. "By the late summer of 92, both Pearl Jam and Soundgarden were so popular with new fans hungry for new material that a tiny side project they'd collaborated on back in 1991 called Temple of the Dog."
facts.source: Hit Parade Music History and Music Trivia
facts.name: Pearl Jam

facts.title: Eddie Vedder, Chris Cornell, and Al Jourgensen – Bile Beer Drinking Contest at Lollapalooza 1992
facts.body: The 1992 Lollapalooza tour featured the Jim Rose Circus sideshow, including performer Matt "the Tube" Crowley, who would pump beer, ketchup, chocolate, and Pepto-Bismol into his stomach via a seven-foot swallowed tube and then pump it back out as "bile beer" for audience members to drink. Eddie Vedder, Chris Cornell (Soundgarden), and Al Jourgensen (Ministry) entered a competition for who could drink the most bile beer. Cornell tried and retched; Jourgensen managed it two days in a row; Eddie was there every single night and claimed to have drunk two quarts more than anyone. When asked why, Eddie said: "Just looking for attention." "Eddie won this contest. He called it Wayne."
facts.source: The Ongoing History of New Music
facts.name: Pearl Jam

facts.title: Lollapalooza 1992 Main Stage Act
facts.body: Pearl Jam was among the major bands performing on the main stage of the 1992 Lollapalooza Festival, a lineup described as one of the best in the event's history. "Sound garden, Pearl Jam, ministry, ice cube. That was just the main stage."
facts.source: The Ongoing History of New Music
facts.name: Pearl Jam

facts.title: Regurgitation Cocktail Drinking Contest (1992)
facts.body: During the 1992 Lollapalooza tour, Eddie Vedder engaged in a drinking contest with Chris Cornell, consuming a cocktail of goo, bile, and Matt "The Tube" Crowley's half-digested last meal, which Crowley had regurgitated on command from a seven-foot hose. Eddie Vedder famously won this contest. "And for the record and for all time, Eddie won this contest."
facts.source: The Ongoing History of New Music
facts.name: Pearl Jam

facts.title: Singles Cameo (1992) – Eddie, Stone, and Jeff as Citizen Dick Members
facts.body: In Cameron Crowe's Seattle-set film *Singles* (filmed 1991, released 1992), Eddie Vedder, Stone Gossard, and Jeff Ament appear as the backing band for fictional singer Cliff Poncier (played by Matt Dillon), in a band called Citizen Dick. Their longest appearance is just over a minute, showing them reading a review of their record. By the time the film was released, Pearl Jam was enormous, which worked greatly in the film's favor. Pearl Jam also contributed two songs to the soundtrack: "Breath" and "State of Love and Trust." "By the time the movie was released in 1992, the band was huge."
facts.source: The Ongoing History of New Music
facts.name: Pearl Jam

facts.title: Singles Soundtrack Contribution (1992)
facts.body: Songs from Pearl Jam were heavily played on the radio and in alternative clubs throughout late 1992, following the release of *Singles*. The movie and its soundtrack were instrumental in expanding the reach and popularity of grunge music. "Songs from Allison Chains, Pearl Jam, The Screaming Trees and The Smashing Pumpkins were all played on the radio and in alternative clubs."
facts.source: The Ongoing History of New Music
facts.name: Pearl Jam

facts.title: Popularity in Late 1992
facts.body: By late summer 1992, Pearl Jam's popularity had surged, contributing to the success of Temple of the Dog, a side project they collaborated on in 1991. The tribute album broke into the top 10 of the album chart and belatedly achieved platinum status. "By the late summer of 92, both Pearl Jam and Soundgarden were so popular with new fans hungry for new material that a tiny side project they'd collaborated on back in 1991 called Temple of the Dog."
facts.source: Hit Parade Music History and Music Trivia
facts.name: Pearl Jam

facts.title: SNL Pope John Paul II Photo Tear (October 3, 1992) – Career-Ending Television Moment
facts.body: After a series of controversies (refusing to appear on SNL while Andrew Dice Clay was host in 1990; refusing the national anthem before a New Jersey show in August 1990; skipping the 1991 Grammys despite four nominations; a perceived pro-Saddam comment in March 1991), Sinead O'Connor appeared on *Saturday Night Live* on October 3, 1992, singing Bob Marley's "War." In rehearsal she held a picture of a refugee child; live, she substituted a photo of Pope John Paul II — taken from her mother's bedroom wall — and tore it up at the word "evil," saying "fight the real enemy." There was complete silence from the studio audience. NBC received nearly 5,000 complaints and the resulting media blowback permanently ended her mainstream career. The inspiration was Bob Geldof tearing up a picture of John Travolta on *Top of the Pops* in the 1970s. "NBC received almost 5,000 complaints. The blowback in the media was intense and her career never, ever recovered."
facts.source: The Ongoing History of New Music
facts.name: Sinead O'Connor

facts.title: Saturday Night Live Pope Photo Tearing (1992)
facts.body: On October 13, 1992, as a musical guest on *Saturday Night Live*, Sinead performed an a cappella version of Bob Marley's "War" instead of her scheduled second song. During the performance, she held up a picture of Pope John Paul II (found on her mother's wall after her death) and tore it to pieces, declaring, "Fight the real enemy." This act, which she stated was planned to destroy a symbol of "lies and liars and abuse" associated with the Catholic Church and her mother, generated immense controversy. "Instead, she held up her mom's picture of the Pope and tore it to pieces."
facts.source: The Ongoing History of New Music
facts.name: Sinead O'Connor

facts.title: SNL Fallout and CD Steamrolling (1992)
facts.body: The Pope photo incident led to immediate and intense backlash: she was egged outside Rockefeller Center, NBC received nearly 5,000 complaint calls, and she was banned from the network. A pile of her CDs and tapes were publicly steamrolled outside her New York record company's offices, an event she and a friend found amusing enough to attend in disguise and even be interviewed by a local reporter. "A pile of her CDs and tapes were literally steamrolled in front of the offices of her New York record company."
facts.source: The Ongoing History of New Music
facts.name: Sinead O'Connor

facts.title: Career Reassessment after SNL (1992)
facts.body: Sinead viewed the *Saturday Night Live* incident not as a derailment, but as a corrective course for her career. She believed having a number one record had "derailed" her, and tearing the photo put her "on the right track," allowing her to embrace her role as a protest singer and perform live without the pressures of pop stardom or compromise. "I feel that having a number one record derailed my career, and my tearing of the photo put me on the right track."
facts.source: The Ongoing History of New Music
facts.name: Sinead O'Connor

facts.title: Saturday Night Live Pope Tearing (1992)
facts.body: On October 3, 1992, as the musical guest on *Saturday Night Live*, Sinéad O'Connor tore up a picture of Pope John Paul II during her a cappella performance of Bob Marley's "War." She did this at the exact moment she sang the word "evil," tossing the pieces towards the camera and saying, "Fight the real enemy," to protest child abuse in the Catholic Church. "But when the show went live, she held up a picture of Pope John Paul II, which she then proceeded to tear up as a way of protesting against child abuse within the Catholic Church."
facts.source: The Ongoing History of New Music
facts.name: Sinead O'Connor

facts.title: Early Financial Struggles (1992)
facts.body: Despite releasing a well-selling debut album, touring extensively, and playing successful concerts, Blur found themselves completely ruined and deeply in debt by mid-1992. This situation, now seemingly unthinkable, was a common problem due to "shameful" record contracts of the era, which also affected bands like The Smiths, who despite many albums and concerts, earned very little.

facts.title: Four-Year Album Gap Explanation (1992-1996)
facts.body: The significant four-year delay between Rage Against the Machine's debut album and their second record, Evil Empire, was attributed to three main factors: extensive touring, side projects (like recording movie soundtracks), and internal political dissension. This delay was unusual for a band whose debut was considered a "game changer," as maintaining momentum typically required a second album within 18 months. "First they toured and toured and toured. Second they got sidetracked on some non-album projects like recording songs for movie soundtracks. And third, internal politics."
facts.source: The Ongoing History of New Music
facts.name: Rage Against The Machine

facts.title: Eccentric Behavior and Sunday Night Live Incident (1992)
facts.body: During the tour for "Blood Sugar Sex Magik," John Frusciante exhibited increasingly erratic behavior, including bringing his guitar to meals, chain-smoking, and shaving his head on a whim. He broke a significant band rule by bringing his girlfriend on the European leg of the tour. A pivotal moment occurred during the band's "Saturday Night Live" performance when Anthony Kiedis believed Frusciante sabotaged their set, particularly during "Under the Bridge," where his guitar playing was described as "woozy and weird," and he blasted his guitar and vocals dissonantly at the end. Kiedis suspected Frusciante was on heroin during the performance. "John was experimenting the way he would have if we'd been rehearsing the tune. Well, we weren't. We were on TV in front of millions of people."
facts.source: The Ongoing History of New Music
facts.episode: The Long Strange Trip of John Frusciante Part 1
facts.name: John Frusciante

facts.title: First Departure from Red Hot Chili Peppers (May 7, 1992)
facts.body: After escalating tensions, interviews he hated, and feeling reduced to a "performing monkey," John Frusciante refused to go on stage at Sonic City in Japan on May 7, 1992, just minutes before a show was to begin. He declared, "I quit," citing an inability to do justice to his creations and hearing voices telling him to leave. Although he reluctantly played that final, poor-quality 15-song set, it marked his last show with the Chili Peppers for six years. The band explained his departure as an inability to cope with mental stress. "I've reached the stage where I cannot do justice to what I've created. I can't give you what it takes to be in this band anymore."
facts.source: The Ongoing History of New Music
facts.episode: The Long Strange Trip of John Frusciante Part 1
facts.name: John Frusciante

facts.title: Post-Quitting Reflection and Life as a Junkie (1992-1996)
facts.body: After leaving the Red Hot Chili Peppers in 1992, John Frusciante auditioned for the Meat Puppets, but it didn't work out. He subsequently fell into a deep depression, becoming a full-fledged heroin addict. At 23, he felt his life and music career were over, and he didn't pick up a guitar for a period. For three years, he rarely left his Hollywood home, which deteriorated, covered in graffiti. He used heroin heavily, stating he was "proud to be an addict" and happy only when on drugs. He neglected to cash royalty checks, including one for $600,000, found by Flea's daughters. "I was very sad and I was always happy when I was on drugs. Therefore I should be on drugs all the time."
facts.source: The Ongoing History of New Music
facts.episode: The Long Strange Trip of John Frusciante Part 1
facts.name: John Frusciante

facts.title: First Departure and Heroin Addiction (1992-1998)
facts.body: In May 1992, in the middle of a tour of Japan, John Frusciante quit the Red Hot Chili Peppers due to becoming angry and disillusioned with fame. For the next six years, he descended into a severe heroin addiction and abject poverty, which led to a house fire and health issues that nearly killed him. "So in May 1992, in the middle of a tour of Japan, he quit, and for the next six years, he slid into a terrible heroin addiction and abject poverty."
facts.source: The Ongoing History of New Music
facts.episode: The Long Strange Trip of John Frusciante Part 2
facts.name: John Frusciante

facts.title: Eccentric Behavior and Sunday Night Live Incident (1992)
facts.body: During the tour for "Blood Sugar Sex Magik," John Frusciante exhibited increasingly erratic behavior, including bringing his guitar to meals, chain-smoking, and shaving his head on a whim. He broke a significant band rule by bringing his girlfriend on the European leg of the tour. A pivotal moment occurred during the band's "Saturday Night Live" performance when Anthony Kiedis believed Frusciante sabotaged their set, particularly during "Under the Bridge," where his guitar playing was described as "woozy and weird," and he blasted his guitar and vocals dissonantly at the end. Kiedis suspected Frusciante was on heroin during the performance. "John was experimenting the way he would have if we'd been rehearsing the tune. Well, we weren't. We were on TV in front of millions of people."
facts.source: The Ongoing History of New Music
facts.episode: The Long Strange Trip of John Frusciante Part 1
facts.name: John Frusciante

facts.title: First Departure from Red Hot Chili Peppers (May 7, 1992)
facts.body: After escalating tensions, interviews he hated, and feeling reduced to a "performing monkey," John Frusciante refused to go on stage at Sonic City in Japan on May 7, 1992, just minutes before a show was to begin. He declared, "I quit," citing an inability to do justice to his creations and hearing voices telling him to leave. Although he reluctantly played that final, poor-quality 15-song set, it marked his last show with the Chili Peppers for six years. The band explained his departure as an inability to cope with mental stress. "I've reached the stage where I cannot do justice to what I've created. I can't give you what it takes to be in this band anymore."
facts.source: The Ongoing History of New Music

facts.title: Daft Punk Origins – Darlin' 1992; Melody Maker Called Them "Daft Punky Trash"; Became Daft Punk
facts.body: Guy-Manuel de Homem-Christo (full first name: Guillaume Manuel) is from just west of Paris; his great-great-grandfather was a famous Portuguese military figure and his grandfather a famous Portuguese poet. Thomas Bangalter is from Paris; his father was a songwriter and record producer and Thomas started piano at age six. The two met in high school in 1987 and formed the rock band Darlin' (named from a Beach Boys song they covered) in 1992. Darlin' recorded four songs, played two gigs, and lasted six months before dissolving after a Melody Maker review called them "daft punky trash" — that phrase became their new name. The third member of Darlin', Laurent Boutonnat, went on to work with Phoenix. "Owing to that snarky review and melody maker, they started Daffed punk."
facts.source: The Ongoing History of New Music
facts.name: Daft Punk

facts.title: Singles (1992) – Walk-On Cameo and Spoonman Song Origin
facts.body: Director Cameron Crowe cast Cornell in a brief, non-speaking walk-on role in *Singles* (1991, released 1992), appearing after a scene where Matt Dillon shows Bridget Fonda his new car stereo, immediately preceding a Soundgarden concert sequence. facts.title: Cameo in Singles (1992)
facts.body: Chris Cornell made a cameo appearance in the 1992 Hollywood motion picture *Singles*. The film was significant for not only featuring the music of the moment but also including appearances from prominent bands and figures of the burgeoning alternative and grunge scene, helping to expand grunge's reach. "It was a Hollywood motion picture that not only featured the music of the moment, but also cameos from Pearl Jam and Chris Cornell and Allison Chains."

facts.title: Formation of Murder Records (Early 1992)
facts.body: Sloan established their own record label, Murder Records, in early 1992, to release their debut EP "The Peppermint-eaky" and bypass the extended timelines of major labels like Geffen/DGC, which projected a much later release date for their first album. The label allowed them to quickly put out music, facilitate touring, and later expanded to release records for other Halifax bands, fostering a communal scene. "So that's why we started murder records was just to put out that EP. And then there was other bands that we knew of that we were friends with."
facts.source: The Ongoing History of New Music
facts.episode: Sloan In Their Own Words: Part 1
facts.name: Sloan

facts.title: Lollapalooza 1992 Main Stage Act
facts.body: Ministry was one of the major bands performing on the main stage of the 1992 Lollapalooza Festival, which was recognized for its "absolutely awesome" lineup, arguably the best in the event's history. "Ministry. One of the bands to perform in the legendary 1992 Lala Pulusa Festival, arguably the best lineup in the history of that event."
facts.source: The Ongoing History of New Music
facts.name: Ministry

facts.title: Al Jorgensen's Backstage Antics (Lollapalooza 1992)
facts.body: At a stop on the 1992 Lollapalooza tour, Ministry's leader, Al Jorgensen, was observed throwing furniture (table, lamps, couch, chair, carpet) out of his backstage trailer. He then carried a broken bottle of Bushmills whiskey, taking long swigs despite its jagged neck. Jorgensen then enlisted help to re-arrange the discarded furniture on the concrete outside his trailer, creating an impromptu "living room," and attempted to share his broken bottle of whiskey. "The last thing to come out of the trailer was Al Jorgensen, the leader of ministry. And he was carrying this broken bottle of Bush Mills whiskey."
facts.source: The Ongoing History of New Music
facts.name: Ministry

facts.title: Lollapalooza "Party in a Bottle" Incident (1992)
facts.body: Backstage at Lollapalooza in 1992, Al Jourgensen forced someone to drink from a bottle of Bushmills whiskey with a broken, jagged neck, threatening physical harm if they refused. It was later revealed that Jourgensen was known to add a "dollop of acid" to his Bushmills, creating what he referred to as a "party in a bottle," though this particular addition fortunately did not occur that day. "I ended up backstage with Al at Lala Paloza in 1992 and he made me drink from a bottle of bush mill whiskey that had dropped on the pavement."
facts.source: The Ongoing History of New Music
facts.name: Ministry

facts.title: Grammy Nomination (1992)
facts.body: Ministry received a Grammy Award nomination in 1992, indicating their increasing recognition and success within the music industry, even though they ultimately lost to Nine Inch Nails. "Ministry was even nominated for a Grammy Award in 1992."
facts.source: The Ongoing History of New Music
facts.name: Ministry

facts.title: Lollapalooza Peak (1992)
facts.body: Ministry was at the forefront of industrial music from 1988 onwards, reaching a peak in 1992 when they were the second-highest billed act on the Lollapalooza tour. "Alan Durgensen and Ministry have been at the forefront, peaking in 1992 when they were second from the top on the Lola Palusatour."
facts.source: The Ongoing History of New Music
facts.name: Ministry

facts.title: Fastest Dance Song (1992)
facts.body: Moby's 1992 track "Thousand" from the B-side of "I Feel It" is in the Guinness Book of World Records as the fastest dance song ever, reaching 1000 beats per minute (BPM). While modern technology allows for compositions up to 15,000 BPM, "Thousand" uniquely achieved a hit single status, reaching number 38 on the British charts, cementing its record. "Moby's Thousand reached number 38 on the British charts."
facts.source: The Ongoing History of New Music
facts.episode: The Book of World Records Version 1.0 - Part 2
facts.name: Moby

"The first Wayne's World CD from 92 is pretty good, although it's mostly classic rock."

facts.title: 1992 MTV Music Video Awards Altercation
facts.body: A backstage confrontation occurred at the 1992 MTV Music Video Awards between Axl Rose, Kurt Cobain, and Courtney Love, where Axl reportedly told Kurt to "keep his woman in line." Separately, Guns N' Roses bassist Duff McKagan and Nirvana bassist Chris Novoselic were also involved in a verbal dispute. "This boiled over to an altercation backstage at the 1992 MTV Music Video Awards between Axel, Kurt and Courtney Love."
facts.source: The Ongoing History of New Music
facts.name: Guns N' Roses

facts.title: 1992 Overdose and Cardiac Arrest
facts.body: In September 1992, while on tour with Metallica, Slash was staying in San Francisco before an Oakland gig. After the Oakland show, drug dealers came to his hotel room at 5 a.m., and Slash took a powerful speedball (heroin and cocaine). He collapsed in the hallway due to cardiac arrest and was technically dead for eight minutes. Paramedics revived him with an adrenaline needle. He was transported to the hospital but quickly signed himself out and was back on stage in Los Angeles two days later. "he'd been technically dead for eight minutes due to cardiac arrest."
facts.source: The Ongoing History of New Music
facts.name: Guns N' Roses

facts.title: Emergence and Characteristics (1992)
facts.body: Jungle emerged around 1992 as a distinct genre, characterized by tempos oscillating between 160 and 170 BPMs, deep bass lines, and strong influences from dancehall and ragga. It was deeply connected to sound system culture and gained popularity in the British scene through pirate radio and illegal parties. "Hacia 1992, de ese caldo de cultivo surgió el jungle."

facts.title: Copenhagen Assault and Irreversible Brain Damage (August 1992)
facts.body: While touring Copenhagen with girlfriend Helena Christensen, Hutchence was sucker-punched by an impatient taxi driver, causing him to fall and hit his head violently on the curb. Although paramedics initially assumed he was on drugs, he sustained severe, irreversible brain damage, which fundamentally altered his personality. "The blow to the head brought something out of Michael and it ended up killing him."
facts.source: The Ongoing History of New Music
facts.name: Michael Hutchence

facts.title: Post-Injury Personality Change and Aggression (1992-1997)
facts.body: Following his brain injury, the previously quiet and gentle Hutchence became aggressive, erratic, and quick to fight, suffering from headaches, vomiting, and a destroyed sense of taste and smell. This change led to rages where he destroyed furniture, damaged a valuable guitar owned by Andrew Farriss, and even threatened bassist Gary Beers with a knife in the studio. "From that point on, the quiet, gentle Michael Hutchins was suddenly different."
facts.source: The Ongoing History of New Music
facts.name: Michael Hutchence

facts.title: 1992 Brit Awards Controversy
facts.body: At the 1992 Brit Awards, The KLF planned extreme stunts, including dumping buckets of blood over the audience and disemboweling a dead sheep on stage, which organizers prohibited. Drummond then threatened to cut off his own hand with an axe, but instead fired blanks over the audience with a machine gun. The purchased sheep was later dumped at an after-party, and their Best Artist trophy was found buried near Stonehenge. "At the 1992 Brit Awards, they plan to dump buckets of blood over the audience and to disembowel a dead sheep on stage. And organizers wouldn't allow that. Drummond said, fight! I'll just cut my hand off with an axon stage. That didn't happen, thankfully. Instead, Drummond showed up with a machine gun and fired blanks over the head of the audience. The sheep, which had already been purchased, was dumped at an after-party. The best artist trophy they won that night was later found buried near Stonehenge."
facts.source: The Ongoing History of New Music
facts.name: The KLF
